title: Two tills at the field station

scenes.title: What will leave the till?
scenes.narration: Two suppliers sell the same waterproof groundsheet, normally forty-eight dollars. The pine counter takes a quarter off. The copper counter takes ten dollars off. The signs name different kinds of saving. Which till would actually take less money for the groundsheet?

scenes.title: Write both till slips
scenes.narration: One quarter of forty-eight dollars is twelve dollars. The pine price is forty-eight minus twelve, or thirty-six dollars. The copper price is forty-eight minus ten, or thirty-eight dollars. Paying thirty-six saves two more dollars. Both slips refer to the same groundsheet.

scenes.title: Different lengths of cord
scenes.narration: Measuring cord for the field kit comes in sealed reels. Eight metres cost six dollars at one counter. Twelve metres cost eight dollars and forty cents at the other. The longer roll costs more to buy. Which counter charges less for each metre? Try comparing an equal length of cord.

scenes.title: Unroll the same length
scenes.narration: Three of the short rolls and two of the long rolls each supply twenty-four metres. Three short rolls cost eighteen dollars. Two long rolls cost sixteen dollars and eighty cents. The long rolls save one dollar and twenty cents on the same length. That is five cents per metre.

scenes.title: Read a faded price ticket
scenes.narration: A faded ticket shows a sale price of thirty-six dollars. Twenty per cent came off the original price. The missing number is the amount before the sale. Does adding twenty per cent of thirty-six reverse the discount? Look at what the thirty-six dollars represents.

scenes.title: Restore the original amount
scenes.narration: Removing twenty per cent leaves four fifths of the original. Across the remaining four equal shares, thirty-six dollars means nine dollars per share. All five shares were worth forty-five dollars. Check forward: twenty per cent of forty-five is nine, and forty-five minus nine is thirty-six.

scenes.title: Count only complete bundles
scenes.narration: A survey team needs ten sample jars, normally three dollars each. The first counter gives five for the price of four. The second takes one dollar and fifty cents off each complete group of three. The last ungrouped jar is full price. Which counter wins this order?

scenes.title: One order, two receipts
scenes.narration: At the first counter ten jars make two groups, each costing twelve dollars. The bill is twenty-four dollars. At the second counter there are three full groups, saving four dollars and fifty cents altogether. The thirty-dollar bill falls to twenty-five dollars and fifty cents. The first counter is cheaper by one dollar and fifty cents.

scenes.title: Circle the unit and the base
scenes.narration: Circle what stays the same when comparing a price: one groundsheet, one metre, or one complete order. For a percentage, circle the amount the percentage belongs to. When a promotion requires groups, count the complete groups and price every leftover item. A final receipt should account for everything bought.
